purpose: Paclitaxel is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including breast cancer, ovarian cancer, lung cancer, and Kaposi's sarcoma. Your doctor prescribes it to help stop cancer cells from growing and spreading in your body.
how_it_works: Think of your cells like they are going through a process of dividing and making copies of themselves. Cancer cells do this out of control. Paclitaxel works by interfering with the tiny internal structures (called microtubules) that cancer cells need to split apart and multiply. By blocking this process, the medicine causes cancer cells to stop dividing and eventually die off.
common_side_effects: Hair loss (very common), numbness or tingling in hands and feet, nausea and vomiting, muscle or joint aches, fatigue and weakness, low blood cell counts (which can make you more prone to infections, bruising, or feeling very tired), and mouth sores. Many of these side effects are temporary and improve after treatment ends.
warnings: Because paclitaxel lowers your white blood cell count, your immune system will be weakened and you will be at higher risk for serious infections — contact your doctor right away if you have a fever, chills, or feel suddenly unwell. Some people have serious allergic reactions during the infusion, so you will be given pre-medications beforehand. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as this medicine can harm a baby. Avoid live vaccines while on treatment. Nerve damage in hands and feet can sometimes be long-lasting, so let your team know if numbness or pain gets worse.
typical_dosing: Paclitaxel is given through an IV (intravenous infusion) in a clinic or hospital — you will NOT take it as a pill at home. The dose and schedule depend on the type of cancer being treated. A common schedule is once every 3 weeks, but some plans use a lower dose given once a week. Each infusion can take 1 to 24 hours. Your oncology team will decide the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
